R4.1.response:
Thank you for setting out exactly what would be convincing; it gave us a concrete programme to follow, and following it changed the paper. We did each of the three things you ask.

On duplicates and near-duplicates, the finding is more serious than a footnote. Before cleaning, the partition contains 446,671 exactly duplicated feature vectors, an 11.06 percent duplicate rate, rising to 12.36 percent among benign flows alone. Under the stratified random split that produced the submitted numbers, 15.49 percent of test rows have a feature-identical twin in the training partition, and a lookup table that learns nothing except the training labels of those twins already reaches 99.28 percent accuracy. Under a chronological split the same lookup reaches 97.14 percent and only 0.04 percent of test rows have a training twin. That difference isolates how much of the submitted performance was available to pure memorization. After deduplication and under the chronological protocol, no test flow has an exact training twin, the median standardized distance from a test flow to its nearest training neighbor is 0.142, and no test flow lies closer than 1e-6.

On feature distributions, no feature has class-disjoint ranges. We also defined the suspect set by measurement rather than by intuition: every feature separating the classes alone at AUC 0.99 or above, of which there are five. Removing all five leaves macro F1 at 97.94 percent against 97.88 percent for the full set, with overlapping bootstrap intervals. Two controls support the rest: a label permutation collapses the pipeline to chance, at macro F1 0.4978 and ROC-AUC 0.5027, and scrambling the arrival order before computing the entropy features drops their individual AUCs from about 0.99 to about 0.56, which confirms the entropy features carry genuine temporal structure rather than a static artifact.

On cross-dataset validation, we evaluated on both corpora you name, with bootstrap confidence intervals on the error rates. The result is negative and we report it as such: zero-shot macro F1 is 0.6026 on InSDN and 0.2788 on CIC-IDS2017, the latter with a false-negative rate of 98.13 percent. We now state that the detector does not transfer across corpora without retraining, and the limitations section says plainly that dataset-specific artifacts cannot be excluded by any experiment available to us on a single synthetic corpus.
R4.1.action: Added a duplicate and near-duplicate analysis across both split protocols with a memorization baseline, a feature-distribution and separability audit with an objectively defined suspect set, two negative controls, and cross-dataset evaluation on InSDN and CIC-IDS2017 with bootstrap intervals on FPR and FNR.
R4.1.location: Sec. VII-D (Leakage and dataset-artifact audit) and its tables; Sec. VII-J (Cross-dataset validation); Sec. IX (Limitations)

R3.4.response:
This question produced one of the more useful findings in the revision, and we are grateful for it, because answering it properly required us to check the premise first. The premise is that a spoofed flood installs one table entry per spoofed source. On this corpus that is not what happens, and we would rather report that than present a reduction we did not observe.

Across the SYN partition, 99.08 percent of the 3,590,794 flows carry a single source address. In the 40,000-flow window replayed through the testbed there are three distinct source addresses spanning two /24 networks. What varies is the port: the same window holds 29,064 distinct destination ports and 34,624 distinct source ports, which is what produces 29,065 distinct exact-match keys from 40,000 flows. The table therefore overflows through the port field, not through the source address.

We measured six aggregation policies at three table capacities under four eviction policies. Exact-match installation saturates the table and overflows continuously, as you anticipate: 913.3 rule installations per thousand flows at a 4,096-entry capacity, with 32,436 overflows. Collapsing the source to a /24 or a /16 changes those figures to four significant figures, because there is no source diversity to collapse, and wildcarding the source entirely changes nothing for the same reason. The policy that bounds the table is the one that wildcards the port: a rule matched on source address, destination address and protocol holds three entries for the whole window, installs 0.07 rules per thousand flows, and never overflows at any capacity we tested. Eviction policy moves the installation count by less than 0.2 percent under every aggregation, so it is second-order on this traffic; the full grid is released with the results.

Two qualifications are stated in the text rather than left implicit. The reduction is bought with specificity, since a port-wildcarded rule also drops legitimate traffic to the same host, so it is an instrument of last resort and the decision of when to escalate to it is a policy question the detector informs but does not settle. And the genuinely source-spoofed case, which source-prefix aggregation exists for, cannot be observed in this export at all, so we measure it separately in the emulated network, where source addresses are randomized at the packet level.
R3.4.action: Added a flow-table occupancy study over six aggregation policies, four eviction policies and three capacities, together with the field-diversity measurements that explain which policy binds, and a statement of the specificity cost of the policy that works.
R3.4.location: Sec. VII-P (Flow-table occupancy under mitigation) and its table; Sec. IV (Architecture); Sec. IX-B
